title: How to Debug a Frontend Error From the First Clue
content:
A blank screen after clicking Save is a clue, not a diagnosis. The most useful first move is to write down exactly what changed: the page, action, account state, browser, time, and visible result. Then reproduce the failure with developer tools open. A repeatable observation lets you distinguish a failed request from a rendering exception, an incorrect response, or a state transition that never happened.

Capture the first reliable clue

Open the browser console, clear old messages, and perform the smallest action that triggers the problem. Chrome's Console reference describes filtering messages, preserving logs, and inspecting the source of errors. Record the first relevant error and its stack, including file and line if a source map is available. Later errors may simply follow from the first one. A stack location is a lead, not proof that the line itself is the root cause.

Write a short reproduction recipe that another developer can follow: start on a named route, use a test account with an identified role, enter safe sample data, press Save once, and observe the result. Remove irrelevant clicks. Note whether the problem occurs on a clean reload, in a private window, or only after navigation. Do not paste tokens, personal data, or full authenticated request bodies into a ticket.

If the error appears only on one device, compare viewport, input method, browser version, and stored site data. If it appears only for one role, compare the actual authorization path. Avoid clearing all caches immediately; doing so can erase the condition you need to explain. Capture evidence first, then test cache or session hypotheses one at a time.

Follow the request, then the response

Use the Network panel to identify the request made by the action. Chrome documents filtering requests and inspecting headers, payloads, responses, timing, and initiators. Check whether the expected request happened at all. No request may mean the click handler did not run, client validation blocked submission, or the app failed before dispatch. A request with an unexpected URL points toward configuration or routing.

Read the HTTP status and response body separately. A 401 or 403 asks an authentication or permission question; a 404 may be an incorrect path or missing resource; a 500 points to server handling but does not identify the cause by itself. Compare the method, content type, and safe field names against the API contract. Inspect a successful request from the same environment if available, while accounting for differences in user role and data.

MDN's Fetch guide explains that fetch resolves on HTTP error statuses and that callers should check response.ok. Code that treats every resolved promise as success may show a confirmation for a failed write. Conversely, parsing every response as JSON can throw if the server returned HTML or no body. Confirm what the client actually did with the response, rather than assuming the status was handled.

Trace the value through the UI

When the request succeeds but the screen remains wrong, follow the returned value through parsing, state update, and rendering. Check the response shape at the boundary. A renamed field, null where a component expects an array, or stale cache key can each produce a plausible but misleading display. Add a temporary breakpoint near the state update and inspect values; do not rely on a screenshot of the final screen alone.

Distinguish the production bundle from the source you are reading. A deployed page may load an older build or a different environment's API base URL. Read the loaded script URL, build identifier if one exists, and source map provenance. A source map helps map compiled code back to source, but it does not guarantee that your local checkout matches the deployed revision. Reproduce against the same build before editing code.

For intermittent failures, record ordering and timing. A component may request data twice, navigate before a write completes, or update state after unmount. Use Network timing and initiator information to reconstruct the sequence. Do not add arbitrary delays as a permanent fix. Find the missing await, cancellation, idempotency control, or state ownership rule that explains the race.

Hypothetical example: a saved profile that looks unchanged

Suppose a hypothetical profile editor shows “Saved” but retains the old display name. The network capture shows one PATCH request, a 409 response, and a JSON body describing a version conflict. The client code awaits fetch, immediately displays success, and never checks response.ok. The visible symptom looks like stale rendering, but the first broken boundary is response handling.

The repair is to branch on the response status, show a conflict message, and let the user reload or reconcile edits. A test should assert that a 409 never yields a success notice and that a successful response updates the displayed name. This example is an illustrative debugging exercise, not a report from a real deployment. Its value is the method: confirm the actual network result before revising component state.

Checklist for a useful fix

  • Write a minimal reproduction with expected and observed results.
  • Save the first relevant console error and request evidence without secrets.
  • Confirm the loaded build and API environment.
  • Check request method, URL, status, response shape, and response.ok handling.
  • Trace successful data through state and rendering.
  • Change one cause, then repeat the same reproduction and a nearby success path.
  • Record the causal explanation in the issue or change review.

Good debugging ends with a causal account, not just a screen that happens to work once. State what failed, why the observed clue led to it, and which verification would catch a recurrence. If the failure remains intermittent, preserve the evidence and narrow the conditions rather than announcing a fix from one successful retry.
excerpt: Trace a frontend failure from a reproducible symptom through console, network, response handling, state, and the loaded build before changing code.
